finding.headline: You plan to retire at 60, so you would wait about 5 years before Medicare starts at 65.
details: Medicare generally starts when you turn 65, and your Initial Enrollment Period lasts 7 months, starting 3 months before you turn 65 and ending 3 months after that month.
If you miss that 7-month window, you may have to wait to sign up and pay a monthly late enrollment penalty for as long as you have Part B coverage, and the penalty rises the longer you wait.
Your 401(k) limit for 2027 is $25,500, and once you reach ages 60 to 63 the higher catch-up limit is $11,750 instead of $8,500, which matters if you save heavily before you retire at 60.

finding.headline: About 33% of your pay goes to tax now; about 16% of withdrawals would go in retirement.
details: Of $310,000 pay, about $101,048 goes to federal, state, and payroll tax, leaving about $208,953.
In retirement, the plan would draw first from taxable savings and cash, then the 401(k), and last from Roth. Tax would be about $27,700 a year.
This is a rough guide, not tax advice. Your 401(k) and IRA limits rise at age 50 and again at age 60 to 63, so check those as you get closer.

finding.headline: You can count on $117,700 a year: $31,100 for basics and $86,600 for the rest.
details: Your basics cost about $31,100 a year.
Your spending goal of $180,000 a year lasts in 37 of 100 scenarios.

assumptions: All figures are in today's dollars: what money buys now, not the larger sums prices will reach.

Savings grow on average 5.0% a year above inflation in stocks and 1.8% in bonds, with good and bad years. The plan tests many possible market paths. These are planning figures, not a forecast. They are fixed, so every plan is tested on the same markets; to see a bad stretch, try a What If such as markets fall 30%.

Until you retire you save about $76,853 a year: $37,400 into a 401(k) or IRA, $9,300 from your employer's match, $30,153 of take-home pay left after your spending, which the plan assumes you save. If that is wrong, change 'Yearly saving' in your answers.
Pay stays at today's level until you retire, with no raises. This is fixed: raises are not certain, so the plan does not count on them. If your pay changes, change it in your answers.
Your spending in retirement leaves out the mortgage. The payments left after you retire, until 2052, are counted as a cost of their own.
Social Security uses the figure you gave, read as the benefit at 67. Your answers show $50,000 a year from 67. This plan starts it at 70, which pays about $62,000 a year.
If you retire before Medicare starts at 65, health cover costs about $10,000 a person a year until then (an assumption). Other health costs follow CMS figures by age.

Tax uses the 2027 federal brackets, the standard deduction and your state's rates. While you work, 401(k) saving comes off taxable pay. In retirement the plan counts 85% of Social Security as taxable, the most the law allows, so the tax may be a little high.
The plan runs to age 95. There is about a 1 in 4 chance that you will live that long (US life table, SOA 2024). People with more money tend to live longer than that table says.
